profile.campus: Chandler, Maricopa County, Arizona (CyrusOne Phoenix-metro campus, PHX1-PHX8)
profile.address: 2495 South Ellis Street, Building 1, Chandler, AZ 85286
profile.reading:
Per CyrusOne's own facility materials and an aggregator listing dedicated to this specific building, PHX4 sits at 2495 South Ellis Street, Building 1, Chandler, AZ 85286, part of CyrusOne's roughly 2,000,000 sq ft, eight-building Chandler campus (PHX1 through PHX8) totaling a publicly stated 169 MW of IT capacity across the whole campus; that campus-wide MW figure is not confirmed as this individual building's own capacity, so it is not asserted here as a single-building number.

Wikipedia's entry on CyrusOne states the company acquired 55.9 acres in Chandler in September 2011 for data center construction, part of its early-2010s national expansion under then-parent Cincinnati Bell before CyrusOne's own 2013 IPO; the company was founded in July 2000 by David Ferdman and Larry Bursten, headquartered in Dallas, Texas, and was taken private in a roughly $15 billion deal when Kohlberg Kravis Roberts (KKR) and Global Infrastructure Partners (GIP) acquired it, closing in March 2022. Chandler's electric and water utility, Salt River Project (SRP), serves this part of the Phoenix metro; Arizona data centers' water-intensive cooling systems have drawn scrutiny from local outlets including the Phoenix New Times given the state's arid climate and ongoing water-supply debates, a regional context relevant to this campus though not a site-specific consumption figure confirmed for this particular building. This registry carries two separate map entities both labeled PHX4 roughly 350 meters apart, most likely a duplicate OSM entry for the same underlying building rather than two distinct facilities; the same confirmed address is applied to both pending a parcel-level resolution.

Chandler's broader appeal to data center operators, alongside CyrusOne, the same submarket has drawn large campuses from other hyperscale and colocation players, stems from Arizona's relatively low natural-disaster risk profile (limited seismic activity, no hurricane exposure), business-friendly tax treatment for data center equipment under state statute, and proximity to fiber routes linking Phoenix to Los Angeles and other West Coast interconnection points, factors industry trade press has repeatedly cited in explaining the Phoenix metro's growth as a secondary US data center hub behind Northern Virginia and Texas.

reading.body:
The Chandler campus PHX1-PHX8 is a consolidated eight-building complex totaling roughly 2 million square feet and 169 MW of published IT capacity spread across the full campus, making it the fifth-largest published data center footprint in Arizona. The individual building PHX4 cannot be isolated from this figure based on published specifications, so its contribution to the campus total is not separately quantified here. At an assumed 40 kW per rack for AI training density, the full campus 169 MW translates roughly to 4,225 racks, though this calculation depends on actual tenant configuration.

The campus holds TIA 942 Class 4 certification and select Energy Star designation, qualifying it for mission-critical workloads requiring high availability and efficient power delivery. The facility sits on roughly 56 acres acquired in 2011, part of CyrusOne's early-2010s national build-out before the company's 2013 IPO and subsequent 2022 acquisition by KKR and Global Infrastructure Partners.

Chandler's appeal to data center operators rests on Arizona's low seismic and hurricane risk, favorable state tax treatment for data center equipment, and position on fiber routes linking Phoenix to the Los Angeles interconnection hub and other West Coast points. The Phoenix metro hosts multiple large hyperscale and colocation campuses, establishing it as a secondary US data center cluster behind Northern Virginia and Texas. Local water-intensive cooling demands reflect broader tension with Arizona's arid climate and contested water supply, though site-specific consumption figures for this building are not published.
